# That cheap GPU-hour comes with hardware ownership

DeepInfra’s latest reprice makes its managed-ownership offer look tempting. Compare the commitment before comparing the hourly rate.

...

Not a product rendering.

## The new price makes the old distinction matter

DeepInfra’s GPU-hour increase, reported by UsagePricing on October 22, reaches the cheaper end of its custom-model hosting range: A100 rises from $0.89 to $1.49, while B200 moves from $3.69 to $4.89. Those are roughly 67% and 33% increases. The current rates are confirmed on DeepInfra’s own page; the previous rates and change timing come from the tracker’s dated evidence, rather than a vendor announcement. Change record; current pricing.

A B200 kept running for a 720-hour month now totals $3,520.80 in compute, an $864 increase against the reported previous rate. DeepInfra’s separate instance page confirms $4.89/hour for one B200, with 180GB GPU memory, 16 CPU cores, 250GB host RAM and 2TB SSD. That is a concrete rental configuration to test, though a listing does not prove available capacity. Instance specification.

...

Alongside hourly rental, DeepInfra advertises DeepCluster B300 capacity at $2.99 per GPU-hour over three years, or $1.98 over five. Read the ownership terms: the customer owns the equipment from day one, while DeepInfra procures, deploys and operates it. The advertised cost includes hardware amortization, datacenter, power and management; storage is optional. This is managed ownership presented in hourly units. DeepCluster terms.

...

- UsagePricing — October 22 change report and dated captures
- DeepInfra — current custom-model GPU rates
- DeepInfra — on-demand B200 instances and included resources
- DeepInfra — DeepCluster ownership, terms and pricing

Checked October 26, 2026. Historical changes are attributed to UsagePricing; current offers were checked against the provider. Calculations and purchasing guidance are editorial analysis. No performance benchmark was run.

results.title: Hidden FLOPs on consumer cards, and the GPU-hour getting dearer — cere-bro
highlights:
Sources:

- Zagitta/gpu-unlock (GitHub README, v1.0.0), surfaced on the X Following feed via @lxfater
- DeepInfra pricing email, received 2026-10-25 (`raw/gmail/2026-10-26-newsletters.md`), pricing page
- The Information: data center late fees hit $5M+ per day (`raw/rss/`)
- AI Weekly, 2026-10-25 (CNBC figures on Nvidia's neocloud exposure and CoreWeave credit default swaps)
- X feed: Nscale filing and lead times, DRAM/substrate lead times, CoreWeave funding gap, Musk on neocloud debt Topic: GPU hardware, compute economics

## TL;DR

Two stories about the price of a FLOP. gpu-unlock is a Linux kernel module that runs before the NVIDIA driver binds an Ampere GeForce card (GA102/103/104/106), uses a known firmware-unlock technique to write the protected "speed selector" registers, then hands the card to the unmodified driver. The effect is to double the issue rate of FP16/BF16-input, FP32-accumulate tensor instructions, a rate NVIDIA keeps at half on GeForce versus the professional parts built on the same silicon. On a 3090 Ti at 450 W, dense BF16 GEMM goes from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS and TF32 from 42.6 to 82.6; user reports on 3090, 3080, 3070 and 3060 show +25% to +81%, lowest on power-capped cards. Real workloads gain less: LLM prefill +14-36%, while decode (memory-bandwidth bound) and INT8 do not change. Outputs were bit-identical before and after. Meanwhile, rented compute is getting more expensive. DeepInfra raises GPU-hour rates on November 9: A100 80GB $0.89 to $1.49 (+67%), H100 $2.20 to $2.90, H200 $2.69 to $3.49, B200 $3.69 to $4.89, B300 $4.89 to $5.89, citing industry-wide hardware cost increases, while serverless per-token prices stay flat. The constraint is upstream of the GPU: Nscale's IPO filing shows about 25,000 active GPUs against 461,000 active and contracted, transformer lead times exceed 160 weeks, and data center tenants now demand $5M+ per day in late-delivery penalties.

results.title: Priced per TB/s, the H200 beats the H100 at 6 of 7 providers | InferPrice
highlights:
2026-11-02 · GPUs Cost Inference 

Decode runs out of memory bandwidth before compute. We priced H100, H200 and B200 per TB/s-hour from NVIDIA specs and 2026-10-30 list prices.

An H200 has exactly as much compute as an SXM H100 and usually rents for more, so on a FLOPS spreadsheet it never makes sense. The H200 vs H100 cost per token question turns on a different column: the H200 moves 4.8 TB/s out of memory against the H100's 3.35, and decode spends its time waiting on memory. Memory is also what the industry is short of: TechCrunch reports that Samsung used its Q2 earnings call to say the shortage worsens in 2027 and stays tight until at least 2028.

So we priced that column, using our GPU table for 2026-10-30.

...

## The table that follows from that

Same provider, same day, SXM H100 against H200 (Vast, Lambda and Baseten list no H200, so they're out):

| Provider | H100 $/h | H200 $/h | H100 $/TB/s-h | H200 $/TB/s-h | B200 $/TB/s-h |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fireworks | 8.00 | 8.00 | 2.39 | 1.67 | 1.62 |
| CoreWeave | 6.16 | 6.31 | 1.84 | 1.31 | 1.07 |
| Nebius | 4.50 | 5.40 | 1.34 | 1.13 | 1.06 |
| Modal | 3.95 | 4.54 | 1.18 | 0.95 | 0.78 |
| DeepInfra | 2.90 | 3.49 | 0.87 | 0.73 | 0.61 |
| RunPod | 3.99 | 5.29 | 1.19 | 1.10 | 1.00 |
| Together AI | 3.99 | 5.99 | 1.19 | 1.25 | 1.02 |

The break-even is 4.8 / 3.35, so the H200 wins per TB/s whenever it costs under 1.43 times the H100. Together AI, at 1.50 times, is the one provider here where it loses. The B200 wins at all seven, and it's the cheapest row at each.

The cheap-looking row is the trap. RunPod's PCIe H100 lists at $2.89, but NVIDIA's product brief gives that card a peak of 2,000 GB/s, so you pay $1.45 per TB/s-hour: more than RunPod's SXM H100, H200 or B200.

results.title: Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16 | GPUJournal
highlights:
Nov 6, 2026

Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Index, November 2026: H100 to B300
highlights:
## Method

- One on-demand price per provider and GPU, taken from public pricing pages or price APIs. Prices for 8-GPU nodes are divided by eight.
- Specialist GPU clouds only for the median. Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle) are listed separately because their prices are 2.5 to 4.5 times higher.
- Monthly cost = hourly price × 730 hours. Prices exclude taxes.

## Median prices by GPU

| GPU | Prices found | Lowest $/h | Median $/h | Median / month |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA B300 | 8 | 6.60 | 8.98 | $6,552 |
| NVIDIA B200 | 11 | 5.43 | 8.19 | $5,979 |
| NVIDIA H200 | 12 | 2.90 | 4.94 | $3,606 |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM | 16 | 1.99 | 3.72 | $2,716 |
| NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 | 9 | 1.40 | 2.19 | $1,599 |
| NVIDIA L40S | 11 | 0.73 | 1.57 | $1,146 |
| AMD MI325X | 2 | 3.80 | 4.21 | $3,071 |
| AMD MI300X | 4 | 2.59 | 3.22 | $2,351 |

...

On-demand prices per GPU-hour at the largest clouds remain far above specialist clouds: H100 from $6.88 (8-GPU instance divided by eight) to more than $12 depending on the provider, and B300 from $15 to $17.80. Commitments of one to three years cut those prices by 30 to 56%.

## What moved in 2026

- Prices are rising again for flagships. At least one large specialist cloud announced increases of 10 to 26% on H100, H200 and B300 from December 1.
- Clusters cost more than single instances. Multi-node offers are commonly 20 to 50% more per GPU than on-demand single servers.
- Listed is not available. Several providers list GPUs with no deployable region, or “contact sales” for every flagship.
- Fees moved to storage and idle time. Egress is mostly free; stopped-instance storage, public IPs and minimum billing periods are where extra cost appears.

results.title: GPU rental prices in 2026: H100, H200 and B200 per hour
results.author: Safeguard Security Team
highlights:
In October 2026, published on-demand list prices for an H100 ranged from about $2 to about $12 per GPU-hour, depending on the provider, the billing model and what is bundled. Specialist clouds mostly sit between $3 and $6. Spot and long commitments can cut the price by half or more. B200 list prices run from about $6 to $14.

...

- AWS Capacity Blocks, p5.48xlarge (8 H100s), N. Virginia, Ohio and Oregon: $47.757 per instance-hour, $5.970 per GPU-hour. AWS Capacity Blocks pricing page, 19 October 2026.
- AWS p5.48xlarge on-demand (8 H100s), N. Virginia, Ohio, Oregon: $6.88 per GPU-hour, as checked by IntuitionLabs on 10 October 2026.
- Azure NC40ads H100 v5 (1 GPU), East US, Linux pay-as-you-go: $6.98 per hour. Azure ND96isr H100 v5 (8 GPUs): $98.32 per VM-hour, $12.29 per GPU-hour. Azure Retail Prices API, 19 October 2026.
- Google Cloud a3-highgpu-8g (8 H100s), Iowa, on-demand: $88.49 per VM-hour, which is $11.06 per GPU-hour. IntuitionLabs, 10 October 2026.
- Oracle Cloud BM.GPU.H100.8: $10.00 per GPU-hour list. IntuitionLabs, 10 October 2026.
- CoreWeave HGX H100, 8 GPUs, on-demand: $49.24 per instance-hour, about $6.16 per GPU. CoreWeave pricing page, 19 October 2026.
- Lambda H100 SXM, 8-GPU instance: $3.99 per GPU-hour. Lambda pricing page, 19 October 2026. IntuitionLabs records $2.99 in a 2025 snapshot.
- Runpod H100 SXM: $3.99 Secure Cloud and $2.69 Community Cloud. H100 PCIe: $1.99 Community Cloud. Runpod pricing page, 19 October 2026.
- Nebius HGX H100 on demand: $4.50 per GPU-hour. Nebius prices page, 19 October 2026. IntuitionLabs says this took effect on 1 October 2026, up from $3.85.
- H200 on-demand list prices: $5.29 (Runpod Secure Cloud), $5.40 (Nebius), about $6.31 (CoreWeave, $50.44 per 8-GPU instance). Provider pages, 19 October 2026.
- B200 on-demand list prices: $6.69 (Lambda, 8 GPUs), $7.99 (Runpod Secure Cloud), $8.50 (Nebius), $8.60 (CoreWeave, $68.80 per 8-GPU instance). AWS Capacity Blocks: $14.208. Provider pages, 19 October 2026.
- B200 index price: $2.31 per hour in early March 2026 and $4.95 in late April 2026, per the Ornn Compute Price Index as reported on tomtunguz.com on 27 April 2026.

...

The IntuitionLabs survey says plainly that its entries mix prepaid capacity, on-demand VMs, pods, and cluster and node rates, and are not interchangeable. Its inclusion rule is publicly displayed hourly rates for a matching product, taken from first-party pages, with promotional rates excluded. It is a survey by one publisher, not an official price index, and its method is as the publisher describes it.

...

Several of these went up. According to the survey, AWS Capacity Blocks rose from $5.19 to $5.97, Runpod Secure Cloud H100 SXM from $3.29 to $3.99, Lambda's 8-GPU SXM from $2.99 (a 2025 snapshot) to $3.99, and Nebius's HGX H100 from $3.85 to $4.50 effective 1 October 2026. The current figures match the providers' own pages on 19 October 2026. The survey says AWS on-demand and Azure list prices were not re-verified as lower than the 2025 third-party figures.

...

## H200 and B200

The H200 is a later Hopper chip with more and faster memory, about 141 GB of HBM3e per GPU on AWS's P5e and P5en instances. The B200 is NVIDIA's Blackwell generation GPU; Lambda's page lists it with 180 GB of memory.

First-party list prices on 19 October 2026 give a clearer picture than earlier in the year:

- H200 on-demand: Runpod Secure Cloud $5.29 and Community Cloud $3.59; Nebius $5.40; CoreWeave $50.44 per 8-GPU instance, about $6.31 per GPU.
- H200 Capacity Blocks on AWS: $6.866 per GPU-hour on p5e.48xlarge and $7.895 on p5en.48xlarge, in the US regions listed.
- B200 on-demand: Lambda $6.69 per GPU on an 8-GPU instance and $6.99 for one GPU; Runpod Secure Cloud $7.99 and Community Cloud $5.98; Nebius $8.50; CoreWeave $68.80 per 8-GPU instance, about $8.60 per GPU.
- B200 Capacity Blocks on AWS: $113.666 per instance-hour, $14.208 per GPU-hour, on p6-b200.48xlarge.
- B200 clusters on Lambda: $9.86 per GPU for 16 GPUs, $9.36 for 64 and $8.87 for 256 or more, for terms of two weeks to a year.

AWS's Capacity Blocks page says its rates are updated regularly, with the next update scheduled for January 2027, and that a block is charged at the rate in effect when it is bought.

The index view is different. The Ornn Compute Price Index, reported in a post dated 27 April 2026 on tomtunguz.com, put the B200 at $4.95 per hour that week, up from $2.31 in early March, a 114% rise in six weeks. The author also reports that the B200 premium over H200 fell to $0.28 per hour in November 2025 and widened to $1.80 by late April 2026. That is one index, from one author, describing a spot style market, so its levels sit below most on-demand list prices. The takeaway is directional: Blackwell prices were rising in spring 2026, and the gap to the previous generation was widening.
